label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
**4 out of 5 stars — a real improvement, with a few things to know**

We paid $2,140 for the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026, plus $95 for the wall mount. That is a substantial purchase for a small congregation, and I would buy it again. I would not, however, tell every small church that it needs one.

We had been livestreaming worship with a webcam since 2020. Our setup is still fairly modest: an old office PC running OBS, streaming to YouTube, with 30–60 viewers most Sundays. The PT-20 did not require us to replace that whole arrangement, which mattered.

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. The 20x optical zoom lets us get useful pictures of the pulpit, altar and other places without everything looking distant. It supports 1080p60, NDI HX and ordinary HDMI output. I have learned what those terms mean, but I am a pastor, not an AV engineer. The practical attraction of PoE was simpler: one cable up to the balcony rather than having to arrange separate power there.

We have nine presets saved: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide view, and two views of the chancel steps. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, operates it from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. Once the views were set up, Sunday operation became quite manageable.

Getting to that point was not entirely smooth. On the first Sunday, the presets had drifted a few degrees by the sermon. A camera that no longer points quite where you saved it is frustrating during worship. Firmware update 2.4 in March fixed that problem for us. The manual is thin and badly translated, so I would not count on it to answer every setup question. Marcy at Chancel AV was excellent on the phone. Her help made a considerable difference.

The picture is a clear improvement over our webcam, especially from the back of a long church. Delores, who is 82 and homebound, called to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That was a better measure of the purchase for me than the specifications.

Low light still has limits. At our Easter Vigil in April, during the first “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today” with only candles, the picture became grainy, but it remained usable. Our old webcam would have shown little more than dots. Do not expect a bright, perfectly clean picture in candlelight, but this was a meaningful improvement.

Autofocus is another limitation. When someone walks between the camera and the pulpit, it can hunt for focus. We now lock focus on the presets rather than leaving it to make that decision during the service.

Most importantly, this camera did nothing to fix our sound problem. Audio is not its job. If people cannot hear your readers or understand the sermon, buying a better camera will not solve that.

My rating is **4 out of 5 stars**. It has made worship easier to follow for people at home, and we would buy it again. But for a congregation under 100, something cheaper may be entirely adequate. I would look carefully at the distance involved, the lighting, and what your present camera actually fails to show before spending this much.
